analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal student aid to colleges whose degree programs don't qualify graduates for the professional licenses they advertise.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan-lite Democratic sponsorship in 2019, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make colleges ineligible for federal student aid — including Pell Grants and federal loans — if they offer a program meant to prepare students for a licensed profession (like nursing) unless graduates are actually qualified to sit for the licensing exam in the states where the school recruits them, and the school arranges the required clinical placements or internships. It would also require colleges to certify annually that their job-training programs meet accreditation and licensure prerequisites, warn students in writing before enrolling them in programs that do not, and make online programs answer to the states where their students live.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — disproportionately working adults and veterans — who enroll in programs at for-profit and online colleges leading to licensed jobs. They would no longer be able to use federal grants and loans for programs whose degrees don't qualify them for the license the program promises, and would get a written warning before knowingly enrolling in a deficient program. Taxpayers benefit too, since they backstop student loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students at career and online colleges

how_it_helps.text: Colleges offering programs meant to lead to licensed professions (nursing, teaching, cosmetology, and similar fields) would lose access to federal student aid unless completing the program actually qualifies graduates to sit for the required licensure exam in every state where the school advertises or enrolls students.
Institutions would have to provide timely clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships — the pre-licensure requirements that for-profit online programs frequently fail to arrange.

Before enrolling a student in a gainful employment program that does not meet a state's licensure prerequisites, the school must tell the student and obtain a signed, handwritten statement that the student still wishes to enroll.
Colleges offering distance education would have to be legally authorized in every state where their enrolled students live, closing a gap that let online programs operate outside state oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — particularly for-profit and online institutions — that run licensing-track programs which fail state accreditation or licensure prerequisites; they would lose federal aid revenue for those programs and face new certification and paperwork duties. Some students in those programs could lose access to aid for schools they knowingly chose.

drawbacks.text: The licensure-qualification requirement applies state by state, so institutions would have had to tailor programs to every state's licensing rules where they recruit students, a real compliance cost, especially for online schools.

The bill requires a student's written acknowledgment before enrolling in a program that fails a state's licensure prerequisites — acknowledging that some students, fully informed, would still enroll in programs leading nowhere, which the warning itself does not fix.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — cutting off federal money for programs whose graduates cannot get licensed — would have been substantial for students and taxpayers, and the compliance burden on legitimate schools was modest since most programs already meet licensure prerequisites. The main cost is a small risk that some students, with full warning, would lose access to programs they would knowingly have chosen anyway. On balance a sound consumer-protection bill, but it never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh those trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate education committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 21, 2019 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges, especially for-profit and online schools, whose programs can keep taking federal aid without qualifying students for licenses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit and online colleges kept operating unchecked

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats were on the bill and it never advanced far enough for any vote to reveal where the parties stood.

industries.industry: For-profit and online colleges selling programs leading to licensed occupations
industries.note: These schools would lose federal student aid eligibility for programs whose graduates cannot qualify for licensure in the states where they recruit — the core problem the bill targets. Legitimate programs would face new certification paperwork but could comply.

industries.industry: Accrediting agencies and state licensing boards
industries.note: The bill leans on programmatic accreditation and state licensure prerequisites as the test for aid eligibility, raising their role as gatekeepers without paying them.
